generated.body_md:
### Why vigour balance is the whole game

A vine with too much vigour pushes energy into shoots and leaves rather than fruit. A vine starved of vigour can't ripen adequately. The target is a vine in balance — enough leaf area to ripen the crop, not so much canopy that the fruit zone becomes a humid, shaded tunnel.

The practical benchmark most Australian and NZ viticulturists use comes from Richard Smart's point-score system. A well-balanced canopy typically scores:

- Shoot length at harvest: 0.9–1.5 m (longer = excess vigour)
- Lateral shoot development: minimal, one node or fewer
- Exposed leaf area in the fruit zone: >50% of leaves in direct sun
- Canopy gaps: 20–40% of the trellis face open
- Layers of leaves at the fruit zone: ≤2 (more than 4 is a problem)
- Bunch exposure: >50% of bunches with direct light contact

If your canopy scores poorly on three or more of these, fruit composition will suffer — higher pH, lower colour, elevated disease pressure, and flavours that read as herbaceous or jammy depending on the direction of the imbalance.

### Reading the canopy mid-season

The window to act is narrow. By the time you're at 50% veraison, canopy interventions have diminishing returns on that vintage — though they still matter for vine balance heading into dormancy.

Key observations to make at flowering, fruit set, and again at bunch closure:

**Shoot vigour** — internodes longer than 80 mm at the growing tip signal excess nitrogen or water. Check your irrigation schedule and any recent fertigation events.

**Canopy density** — push your hand into the fruit zone. If you can't see daylight through the canopy from the other side, you have a shading problem. This is the fastest field test.

**Lateral growth** — heavy lateral development after fruit set is the canopy's way of telling you it has more energy than it needs. Hedging laterals is a short-term fix; the underlying cause is usually excess water or nitrogen.

**Fruit zone humidity** — dense canopies trap moisture. If you're seeing early botrytis or powdery mildew in the bunch zone before bunch closure, canopy density is almost always a contributing factor.

### Crop level and its relationship to quality

Yield and quality are not automatically in opposition, but there is a real relationship between crop load and the vine's capacity to ripen fruit fully.

The useful metric is yield-to-pruning-weight ratio — the Ravaz Index. A ratio between 5 and 10 generally indicates a balanced vine. Below 5 suggests the vine is under-cropped relative to its vegetative capacity (excess vigour likely). Above 10 suggests the crop is outrunning the canopy's ability to ripen it.

Practical crop management decisions:

- **Green harvest** (crop thinning): most effective before veraison. Removing bunches after veraison has limited impact on berry composition and wastes the vine's investment in those bunches.
- **Timing matters more than volume**: removing 20% of the crop at fruit set has a larger compositional effect than removing 30% at veraison.
- **Whole-bunch vs. berry thinning**: removing entire bunches is more efficient and less likely to cause compensatory berry swelling in the remaining fruit.
- **Don't chase a yield target in isolation**: a 3 t/ha crop on a low-vigour site in a dry year may be perfectly balanced. The same yield on a high-vigour, irrigated site may still be under-cropped.

### Pruning decisions that set up next season

About 90% of the previous season's wood is removed at winter pruning. The retained 10% — whether as spurs or canes — determines bud number, and bud number sets the ceiling on next year's crop before the season even starts.

Light pruning leaves more buds, which typically means more shoots, more crop, and — if vigour is already high — a canopy that's harder to manage. Heavy pruning reduces bud number, concentrates the vine's resources into fewer shoots, and can push vegetative growth if the vine's root system has more capacity than the canopy above it.

The practical rule: match bud number to the site's demonstrated capacity to ripen that crop. If last vintage showed excess vigour (long internodes, heavy laterals, poor fruit zone exposure), reduce bud number at pruning and reassess irrigation and nutrition inputs before budburst.

Spur pruning suits high-vigour sites and mechanised operations. Cane pruning gives more flexibility in bud placement and suits varieties with low basal bud fruitfulness — Chardonnay and Pinot Noir being the obvious examples.

### What to do this vintage

Score your canopy against Smart's benchmarks at bunch closure and record the result in your growing-season log — Owen's prompts will flag the right timing. If you're outside range on shoot length, canopy density, or fruit zone exposure, note the likely cause (water, nitrogen, or pruning weight) so your winter pruning and pre-season nutrition plan addresses the root issue rather than just the symptom.
